name: financial_accounting_set1_p1
label: Financial Accounting: set 1 (foundations, books of original entry, cash book, petty cash, ledger)

papers.title: Introduction to Financial Accounting: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on introduction to financial accounting, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes accounting?
questions.explanation:
Accounting records, classifies, summarises, analyses and interprets financial information and communicates it to users.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- recording transactions in books only: That is bookkeeping, only the first stage of accounting.
- checking the accounts of a business independently: That is auditing.
- calculating the tax a business must pay: That is taxation, one branch of accounting.

options.label: A
options.content: recording, classifying, summarising and interpreting financial transactions

options.label: C
options.content: checking the accounts of a business independently

options.label: D
options.content: calculating the tax a business must pay

questions.stem: A bank considering a loan to a trader is mainly interested in the trader's
questions.explanation:
Lenders use accounts to judge profit, cash flow and security, to decide whether the loan can be repaid.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- number of employees: Staff numbers do not show ability to repay.
- advertising methods: Advertising does not show ability to repay.
- choice of suppliers: Suppliers do not show ability to repay.

options.label: B
options.content: ability to repay the loan and interest

questions.stem: The independent examination of accounting records to give an opinion on whether they are true and fair is
questions.explanation:
Auditors examine the records and financial statements independently and report whether they are true and fair.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- bookkeeping: Bookkeeping is the recording of transactions.
- cost accounting: Cost accounting finds the cost of products and services.
- management accounting: Management accounting provides information for internal decisions.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of the accounting cycle?
questions.explanation:
Each transaction is evidenced by a source document, entered in a book of original entry, posted to the ledger, listed in the trial balance and summarised in the final accounts.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- ledger, source document, trial balance, final accounts: Transactions start with a source document.
- book of original entry, source document, ledger, final accounts: The source document comes before the book of original entry.
- trial balance, ledger, book of original entry, final accounts: The trial balance is prepared from ledger balances.

options.label: A
options.content: ledger, source document, trial balance, final accounts

options.label: B
options.content: book of original entry, source document, ledger, final accounts

options.label: C
options.content: trial balance, ledger, book of original entry, final accounts

options.label: D
options.content: source document, book of original entry, ledger, trial balance, final accounts

questions.stem: The double-entry system was first described in print in 1494 by
questions.explanation:
Luca Pacioli described double entry in 1494 and is often called the father of accounting.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Adam Smith: Adam Smith was an economist who wrote The Wealth of Nations in 1776.
- Isaac Newton: Newton was a physicist and mathematician.
- Karl Marx: Marx was a political economist of the nineteenth century.

papers.title: Accounting Concepts and Principles: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on accounting concepts and principles, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The concept which treats the owner and the business as separate is the
questions.explanation:
Under the business entity concept, the owner's private transactions are kept out of the business records, for example as drawings.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- going concern concept: Going concern assumes the business will continue operating.
- money measurement concept: Money measurement records only items measurable in money.
- dual aspect concept: Dual aspect says every transaction has two effects.

questions.stem: Including unpaid December electricity as an expense of the year ending 31 December applies the
questions.explanation:
The accruals concept records expenses when incurred, not when paid, and matches them with the income of the period.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- consistency concept: Consistency means using the same methods every year.
- historical cost concept: Historical cost is about valuing assets at cost.
- materiality concept: Materiality is about the significance of items.

questions.stem: Valuing inventory at the lower of cost and net realisable value is an application of the
questions.explanation:
Prudence recognises expected losses at once but does not anticipate profits.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- realisation concept: Realisation is about when revenue is recognised.
- business entity concept: Business entity separates owner and business.
- periodicity concept: Periodicity concerns the length of the accounting period.

questions.stem: In 2026 a tailor earned NLe 60,000, of which NLe 52,000 was received. Expenses incurred were NLe 35,000, of which NLe 32,000 was paid. The profit on the accrual basis is
questions.explanation:
Accrual basis: income earned − expenses incurred = 60,000 − 35,000 = 25,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 20,000: That is the cash basis: 52,000 − 32,000.
- NLe 17,000: That mixes cash received with expenses incurred: 52,000 − 35,000.
- NLe 28,000: That mixes income earned with expenses paid: 60,000 − 32,000.

questions.stem: The modern (IFRS) name for the balance sheet is the
questions.explanation:
The balance sheet is called the statement of financial position under IFRS.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- income statement: The income statement replaces the trading, profit and loss account.
- statement of cash flows: That shows cash movements, not assets and liabilities.
- statement of affairs: A statement of affairs is used with incomplete records.

papers.title: The Accounting Equation: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the accounting equation, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The accounting equation is
questions.explanation:
Everything the business owns is financed by the owner (capital) or by outsiders (liabilities).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- Assets = Capital − Liabilities: Liabilities are added to capital, not subtracted.
- Capital = Assets + Liabilities: Capital equals assets minus liabilities.
- Liabilities = Assets + Capital: Liabilities equal assets minus capital.

questions.stem: A business has assets of NLe 145,000 and liabilities of NLe 49,000. Its capital is
questions.explanation:
Capital = assets − liabilities = 145,000 − 49,000 = 96,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 194,000: That adds liabilities to assets.
- NLe 49,000: That is the liabilities figure.
- NLe 145,000: That is the total assets figure.

questions.stem: Buying stock on credit will
questions.explanation:
Stock (an asset) rises and trade payables (a liability) rise by the same amount.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- increase assets and decrease liabilities: Credit purchases add a trade payable.
- decrease assets and increase capital: No asset falls and capital is unchanged.
- increase assets and increase capital: Capital is unchanged; a liability arises.

questions.stem: Opening capital NLe 80,000; capital introduced NLe 10,000; profit NLe 34,000; drawings NLe 18,000. Closing capital is
questions.explanation:
Closing capital = 80,000 + 10,000 + 34,000 − 18,000 = 106,000.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 142,000: Drawings must be deducted, not added.
- NLe 96,000: Capital introduced must be added.
- NLe 124,000: Drawings of 18,000 have been ignored.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a current liability?
questions.explanation:
A bank overdraft is money owed to the bank, repayable on demand: a current liability.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- trade receivables: Trade receivables are a current asset.
- motor vehicle: A motor vehicle is a non-current asset.
- ten-year bank loan: A long-term loan is a non-current liability.

papers.title: Double-Entry Bookkeeping: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on double-entry bookkeeping, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Goods sold on credit to Kamara are recorded by
questions.explanation:
Kamara receives the goods and owes the business (debit Kamara); sales income is credited.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debiting sales and crediting Kamara: That reverses the entry.
- debiting cash and crediting sales: That is a cash sale.
- debiting Kamara and crediting purchases: Purchases records goods bought, not sold.

questions.stem: Wages paid by cheque are recorded by
questions.explanation:
Expenses are debited; the bank, an asset, decreases and is credited.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debiting bank and crediting wages: Money leaving the bank is a credit to bank.
- debiting wages and crediting cash: The payment was by cheque, so the bank account is used.
- debiting capital and crediting bank: Wages are an expense, not a reduction of capital directly.

questions.stem: Under the traditional rules, for real accounts you should
questions.explanation:
Real accounts record things owned: debit what comes in, credit what goes out.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit the receiver and credit the giver: That is the rule for personal accounts.
- debit expenses and credit incomes: That is the rule for nominal accounts.
- debit what goes out and credit what comes in: That reverses the rule.

options.label: A
options.content: debit the receiver and credit the giver

options.label: B
options.content: debit what comes in and credit what goes out

options.label: D
options.content: debit what goes out and credit what comes in

questions.stem: A delivery van bought for use in the business is debited to the
questions.explanation:
A van for business use is a non-current asset with its own real account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- purchases account: Purchases is only for goods bought for resale.
- sales account: Sales records goods sold.
- drawings account: Drawings records the owner's private withdrawals.

questions.stem: Goods returned by a customer, Bah, are recorded by
questions.explanation:
Returns inwards reduce sales (debit); Bah owes less (credit Bah).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debiting Bah and crediting returns inwards: That reverses the entry.
- debiting returns outwards and crediting Bah: Returns outwards are goods returned to suppliers.
- debiting sales and crediting cash: No cash is involved in a return on credit.

options.label: A
options.content: debiting Bah and crediting returns inwards

options.label: B
options.content: debiting returns outwards and crediting Bah

options.label: D
options.content: debiting returns inwards and crediting Bah

papers.topic: Source Documents and Books of Original Entry
papers.title: Source Documents and Books of Original Entry: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on source documents and books of original entry, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: A seller issues a credit note when
questions.explanation:
A credit note reduces the amount the buyer owes because of returns, damage or overcharging.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- goods are sold on credit: Goods sold on credit are billed with an invoice.
- a customer pays in cash: Cash received is evidenced by a receipt.
- the business pays a supplier: A payment is evidenced by a cheque counterfoil or receipt.

options.label: A
options.content: goods are returned or the buyer has been overcharged

questions.stem: Goods listed at NLe 16,500 are sold less 10% trade discount. The amount recorded in the sales day book is
questions.explanation:
Net amount = 16,500 − 10% × 16,500 = 16,500 − 1,650 = 14,850.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 16,500: Trade discount is deducted before recording.
- NLe 1,650: That is the trade discount itself.
- NLe 18,150: Trade discount is deducted, not added.

questions.stem: Trade discount differs from cash discount because trade discount is
questions.explanation:
Trade discount is a reduction from list price for bulk buying or resale and is never entered in the ledger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- given for prompt payment: That describes cash discount.
- recorded in the discount column of the cash book: Only cash discount is recorded there.
- an expense in the income statement: Discount allowed (cash discount) is the expense.

options.label: B
options.content: recorded in the discount column of the cash book

options.label: C
options.content: deducted on the invoice and not recorded in the ledger

options.label: D
options.content: an expense in the income statement

questions.stem: A computer bought on credit for use in the business is first recorded in the
questions.explanation:
Non-current assets bought on credit are recorded in the general journal.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- purchases day book: Day books record goods for resale only.
- cash book: No cash was paid at the time.
- sales day book: The sales day book records credit sales.

questions.stem: The total of the purchases day book is posted to the
questions.explanation:
Each supplier is credited individually; the total is debited to purchases.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- credit side of the purchases account: Purchases (an expense) are debited.
- debit side of each supplier's account: Suppliers are credited individually.
- credit side of the sales account: The sales account receives sales day book totals.

options.label: A
options.content: debit side of the purchases account

options.label: B
options.content: credit side of the purchases account

options.label: C
options.content: debit side of each supplier's account

options.label: D
options.content: credit side of the sales account

papers.title: The Cash Book: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the cash book, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The cash book is both a book of original entry and
questions.explanation:
Transactions are first recorded in the cash book, which also serves as the cash and bank accounts in the ledger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a source document: Source documents are the evidence for entries.
- a trial balance: The trial balance lists ledger balances.
- a final account: Final accounts summarise the year's results.

questions.stem: A customer owing NLe 5,000 pays by cheque less 5% cash discount. The cheque is for
questions.explanation:
Discount = 5% × 5,000 = 250; cheque = 5,000 − 250 = 4,750.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 5,000: The discount of 250 must be deducted.
- NLe 5,250: Discount reduces, not increases, the payment.
- NLe 250: That is the discount itself.

questions.stem: Discount allowed is recorded in the cash book
questions.explanation:
Discount allowed is given to customers when they pay, so it sits beside the receipt on the debit side.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- in the discount column on the credit side: That is where discount received goes.
- in the bank column on the credit side: Discount is not a bank payment.
- only in the general journal: It is recorded in the three-column cash book.

options.label: A
options.content: in the discount column on the credit side

options.label: B
options.content: in the bank column on the credit side

options.label: D
options.content: in the discount column on the debit side

questions.stem: Cash paid into the bank from the office cash is recorded as
questions.explanation:
Both sides of the transaction are in the cash book, marked c, and nothing is posted to the ledger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit cash column, credit bank column: That records cash withdrawn from the bank.
- debit bank column, credit sales: No sale is involved.
- debit capital, credit cash: The owner's capital is not affected.

options.label: A
options.content: a contra entry: debit bank column, credit cash column

options.label: B
options.content: debit cash column, credit bank column

questions.stem: A credit balance on the bank column of the cash book means
questions.explanation:
Paying out more than is in the account creates an overdraft, a liability shown as a credit balance.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the business has money in the bank: Money in the bank is a debit balance.
- cash in hand is overdrawn: The cash column cannot have a credit balance.
- the bank owes the business: When the bank owes the business, the balance is debit.

options.label: A
options.content: the business has money in the bank

options.label: B
options.content: the business has a bank overdraft

papers.title: The Petty Cash Book: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the petty cash book, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: Under the imprest system, the petty cashier is reimbursed
questions.explanation:
Reimbursing exactly what was spent restores the cash in hand to the imprest.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a fixed sum every period regardless of spending: The float is fixed; the reimbursement varies with spending.
- double the amount spent: Only the amount spent is reimbursed.
- the balance left in the petty cash box: The balance is what remains, not what is refunded.

options.label: A
options.content: a fixed sum every period regardless of spending

options.label: C
options.content: the exact amount spent during the period

options.label: D
options.content: the balance left in the petty cash box

questions.stem: An imprest is NLe 5,000 and NLe 700 is left at the end of the month. The reimbursement is
questions.explanation:
Reimbursement = imprest − cash in hand = 5,000 − 700 = 4,300.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- NLe 5,700: The balance left is deducted, not added.
- NLe 700: That is the cash left, not the amount spent.
- NLe 5,000: Only the amount spent is reimbursed.

questions.stem: Every petty cash payment should be supported by a
questions.explanation:
A signed and authorised voucher is the source document for each petty cash payment.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- sales invoice: A sales invoice records credit sales.
- credit note: A credit note records returns or overcharges.
- bank statement: A bank statement records bank transactions.

questions.stem: In an analytical petty cash book, each payment is entered in
questions.explanation:
The total column finds total spending; the analysis column groups it by type.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the receipts column only: The receipts column records money received.
- two analysis columns: Each payment belongs to one type of expense.
- the ledger column only: The ledger column is only for payments to creditors.

options.label: B
options.content: the total column and one analysis column

questions.stem: When the petty cashier is reimbursed by cheque, the entry is
questions.explanation:
Money moves from the bank (credit) to the petty cash float (debit).

**Why the other options are wrong**

- debit bank, credit petty cash book: That reverses the entry.
- debit expenses, credit bank: Expenses are posted from the analysis column totals.
- debit petty cash book, credit capital: Capital is not involved.

options.label: A
options.content: debit bank, credit petty cash book

options.label: C
options.content: debit petty cash book, credit bank in the cash book

options.label: D
options.content: debit petty cash book, credit capital

papers.title: The Ledger: practice set 1
papers.description: 5 original WASSCE-style objective questions on the ledger, each with an explanation and the reason behind every wrong option. Written by WASSCE Tutor, not taken from WAEC papers.

questions.stem: The personal accounts of credit customers are kept in the
questions.explanation:
Customers (trade receivables) are kept in the sales (debtors') ledger.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- purchases ledger: The purchases ledger holds suppliers' accounts.
- private ledger: The private ledger holds confidential accounts such as capital.
- general ledger: The general ledger holds nominal and real accounts.

questions.stem: A customer's account has debits of NLe 7,000 and NLe 4,500 and credits of NLe 800 and NLe 6,000. The balance is
questions.explanation:
Debits 11,500 − credits 6,800 = 4,700, a debit balance: the customer owes the business.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- a credit balance of NLe 4,700: The debit side is larger, so the balance is debit.
- a debit balance of NLe 18,300: Debits and credits have been added together.
- a debit balance of NLe 11,500: Credits have not been deducted.

questions.stem: When balancing an account, the balance carried down is entered on
questions.explanation:
Balance c/d goes on the smaller side so both totals agree; balance b/d goes on the opposite side next period.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the larger side: The balance b/d goes on the larger side, after the totals.
- both sides: It is entered once, then brought down once.
- neither side; it is shown below the totals: It must be entered to make the totals agree.

options.label: D
options.content: neither side; it is shown below the totals

questions.stem: A credit balance on a supplier's account shows that
questions.explanation:
A credit balance on a personal account of a supplier is a trade payable.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- the supplier owes the business: That would be a debit balance.
- the account has been closed: A closed account has no balance.
- goods have been returned: Returns reduce the balance but do not explain it.

questions.stem: The folio column in a ledger account is used to
questions.explanation:
Folio references link each entry to the book of original entry or the other account.

**Why the other options are wrong**

- record the date of the transaction: The date column records the date.
- record the amount: The amount column records the amount.
- show the balance of the account: Balances are calculated, not shown in the folio column.

options.label: A
options.content: record the date of the transaction

options.label: C
options.content: show the balance of the account

options.label: D
options.content: show where the other part of the entry or its source can be found
